title: Case Report: Spontaneous Rupture of Inferior Epigastric Artery Masquerading as Inguinal Hernia
journal: Clinical Practice and Cases in Emergency Medicine
case_prompt:
A 29-year-old male presents to the emergency department with progressive right groin pain and swelling for 24 hours. He reports symptom onset shortly after sexual intercourse. He notes increased tenderness and a persistent bulge in the right groin. He had a normal bowel movement one day before presentation and passed gas on the day of presentation. He denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, dysuria, hematuria, flank pain, penile discharge, testicular pain, or skin lesions.

His medical history is unremarkable; he takes no medications. He smokes cigarettes and drinks alcohol occasionally. He has no history of trauma.

Vital signs: temperature 37.1ºC, pulse 102 beats/min, blood pressure 125/73 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Physical examination is notable for a soft, nontender, nondistended abdomen with normoactive bowel sounds. There is a large, fixed, mildly tender mass in the right groin with no overlying skin changes and no fluctuance; the mass cannot be reduced with gentle pressure. The genital examination is normal.

Laboratory studies show a white blood cell count of 10,740 cells/L, hemoglobin 15.3 g/dL, platelets 233,000 cells/L, and an alanine aminotransferase of 61 IU/L; electrolytes and lactate (1.10 mmol/L) are within normal limits. Urinalysis is unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis reveals a 6.2 × 7.1 × 7.7 cm heterogeneous mass in the right inguinal region with adjacent fat stranding, suggestive of a large hematoma or heterogeneous soft-tissue mass. The mass extends to the groin musculature but does not appear to be related to a hernia sac. Prominent lymph nodes are noted in the right groin.

General surgery is consulted for further evaluation.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Incarcerated or strangulated inguinal hernia considered — “did not appear to be related to a hernia.”  
2. Abdominal wall abscess considered — “no fluctuance noted.”  
3. Tumors of the abdominal musculature considered — “findings suggestive of large hematoma or heterogeneous, soft-tissue mass.”  
4. Mesenteric thrombosis considered — “Lactic acid was normal at 1.10 mmol/L.”  
5. Intestinal obstruction considered — “The abdomen was soft, nontender, nondistended, with normoactive bowel sounds.”  
6. Muscle rupture considered — “unless there is a clear provocation, such as obvious trauma.”  
7. Ovarian cysts considered in the differential of groin masses — “A 29-year-old male presented…”
